Pain Management in Labor
NRBS 3510
SUMMER 2026

Nursing Care Management 
 Plan of care and implementation in 
conjunction with maternal choices
 Nonpharmacologic interventions
 Informed consent for pharmacological 
interventions
 Timing of administration
 Preparation for procedures

Labor Pain Management 
 Cultural Influences-Cultural or religious implications may influence 
desire for pain management
 Prior Experiences-positive birth experience decreases the use of 
medications 
 Preparation-women who have participated in childbirth education 
report better pain management
 Support-women who have a dedicated person providing labor support 
report better pain management and greater satisfaction with birth.  
 DOULA- certified, volunteer or paid individual who is trained to support 
a woman through labor.  Not a midwife
 Positioning-lithotomy position is linked with longer labor and greater 
reported labor pain
 Anxiety-strong correlation between reports of pain and anxiety level
3

Non-pharmacologic Management of Discomfort 
 Nonpharmacologic measures often simple, safe, and 
inexpensive
 Provide sense of control over childbirth and choice of 
measures woman
  Methods require practice for best results
 Try variety of methods and seek alternatives, including 
pharmacologic methods, if measure used is not effective

Non-pharmacologic
 Relaxing and breathing techniques
◦ Relaxation-centered, nurse or partner participation
◦ Imagery and visualization-what is important to patient
◦ Music-maternal choice
◦ Touch and massage-maternal choice
◦ What works at 4cm may not work at 8 cm
◦ Conscious breathing-centering 
◦ Effleurage and counter-pressure
◦ Effleurage is rhythmic and light touch of abdomen with a 
circular motion
◦ Water therapy (hydrotherapy) 
◦ Appropriate only if membranes are NOT Ruptured

Pharmacologic Measures
 Systemic analgesia:  Morphine 
 Regional or local anesthesia: spinal or pundenal 
block
 Epidural: A neuraxial analgesia/anesthesia 
technique, continuously or intermittently into 
epidural or intrathecal space.
 Most common 75% of births in US are with 
epidural 
 Combination of local anesthetic (bupivacaine) and 
opiod (fentanyl)

Systemic Analgesia
 Route: typically administered parenterally through 
existing IV line
 Drugs 
Most commonly used
 Opioids Morphine, Butorphanol (Stadol), 
meperidine (Demerol) 
 Ataractics (hydroxyzine, promethazine)
 Benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam)

Systemic Medications
 Opiods-given in early labor:
 latent phase or active phase up to 7 cms
 Administered IV
 Risk of respiratory depression in neonate
 Morphine
 Stadol
 Nubain
◦ Less respiratory depression 
◦ Lasts longer
 Assess for Respiratory Depression in Mother and Newborn
◦ Duration of 30 minutes to 1.5 hours
9

Regional 
Analgesia/Anesthesia
 Epidural block: continuous infusion or intermittent 
injection; usually started when dilation >5 cm
 Combined spinal-epidural block (“walking epidural”)
 Provides pain blocking while maintaining muscle control
 Patient-controlled epidural-PCA- less common
 Local injection (usually for episiotomy or laceration 
repair)-Lidocaine most common
 Pudendal block (usually for 2nd stage, episiotomy, or 
operative vaginal birth)-pudendal nerve near ischial 
spines-blocks perineal, vulvar or vaginal pain
 Intrathecal (spinal) analgesia/anesthesia (during 
labor and cesarean birth)

Regional Anesthesia Risks and Nursing Care
 Epidural Risks:
 MATERNAL HYPOTENSION
 Pre-medicate patient with 2 Liters IV Fluid 
before placement
 B/P monitoring-before and after placement
 Q 5 min for 15 minutes
 MD/RN Anesthetist must remain at bedside for 
first 15 minutes
 Allergic Reactions
 Respiratory suppression with thoracic 
placement
◦ Reversal of hypotension with ephedrine and 
fluid bolus
◦ Risks to fetus-related to maternal hypotension
◦ Continuous FHR monitoring

Nurse’s Role with Regional Anesthesia
 Assess IV access
 Ensure adequate hydration prior to delivery of anesthesia
 Assess fetal well being before/during/after 
 Assist with positioning of patient for procedure
 Monitor vital signs, esp BP q5 mins after initiation of 
anesthesia, then q15
 Assess progress of labor
 Assess bladder distention
 foley if needed
 Encourage/direct patient to push when indicated
 Request reduction in medication if pushing efforts are 
ineffective
12

General Anesthesia
 Emergency cesarean birth or woman with 
contraindication to use of regional anesthesia
 Spinal surgeries
 Spinal injuries or malformations
 IV injection to produce sedation
 Followed by inhalation- nitrous oxide 
 IV muscle relaxants for paralysis

Nalaxone Hydrochloride 
“Narcan”
 Must have Narcan readily available or at beside 
to reverse opiate actions.
 Maternal 0.4-2mg IV q 2-3 minutes
 Infant: 0.1mg / kg IV or IM Q 2-3 minutes up to 
3 doses
14

Pharmacologic Pain Management
 Contraindications to epidural blocks
 Maternal refusal or inability to cooperate
 Maternal cardiac conditions
 Antepartum hemorrhage
 Anticoagulant therapy or bleeding disorder
 Infection at injection site
 Allergy to anesthetic drug

Pharmacologic Management
of Discomfort—cont’d 
 Direct Spinal Anesthesia
 Used primarily for c-section
 Rapid onset (1-3 minutes)
 Full anesthesia
 Similar risks/contraindications to epidural
 Risk of headache 
17

Pharmacologic Management
of Discomfort—cont’d 
 General anesthesia
 Used rarely for vaginal births
 Infrequently for elective cesarean 
section
 May be necessary if indications 
necessitate a rapid birth or STAT c-
section
